subtitle: Circle (PDF Q41–Q60, numbered 1–20) · detailed solutions

sections.title: Single Correct Type
marking: 4 marks each (JEE Advanced default; no marks printed in the paper)

concepts: Circle touching an axis and intercept on the other axis
General equation of a circle
questions.question: Let the equation of the circle, which touches the $x$-axis at the point $(a,0)$, $a>0$ and cuts off an intercept of length $b$ on the $y$-axis be $x^2+y^2-\alpha x+\beta y+\gamma=0$. If the circle lies below the $x$-axis, then the ordered pair $(2a,b^2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Touching the $x$-axis at $(a,0)$ below it puts the centre at $(a,-r)$; compare coefficients with the general form.
solution: The circle touches the $x$-axis at $(a,0)$ and lies below it, so its centre is $(a,-r)$ with radius $r$.
The centre is at distance $a$ from the $y$-axis; the chord on the $y$-axis has half-length $\frac b2$, so by Pythagoras $r^2=a^2+\frac{b^2}{4}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$: it touches the $x$-axis iff $g^2=c$, and cuts the $y$-axis in a chord $2\sqrt{f^2-c}$.
solution: It touches the $x$-axis at $(-g,0)$, so $a=-g=\frac{\alpha}{2}$, i.e. $2a=\alpha$.

useful_results: For $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$: intercept on the $x$-axis is $2\sqrt{g^2-c}$, on the $y$-axis $2\sqrt{f^2-c}$.
The circle touches the $x$-axis iff $g^2=c$ (touches the $y$-axis iff $f^2=c$), at the point $(-g,0)$.
Instance: with $2g=-\alpha$, $2f=\beta$, $c=\gamma$ the intercept relation reads $b^2=\beta^2-4\gamma$ directly.

concepts: Chord of a circle and its perpendicular bisector
Area of a quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals
questions.question: Let the line $x+y=1$ meet the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ at the points $A$ and $B$. If the line perpendicular to $AB$ and passing through the mid point of the chord $AB$ intersects the circle at $C$ and $D$, then the area of the quadrilateral $ADBC$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The perpendicular through the midpoint of a chord passes through the centre, so $CD$ is a diameter and $CD\perp AB$.
solution: The mid-point of $AB$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $O(0,0)$ on $x+y-1=0$: $\frac{x-0}{1}=\frac{y-0}{1}=-\frac{0+0-1}{2}$.
The line through it perpendicular to $AB$: $y-\frac12=x-\frac12$, i.e. $y=x$. It passes through $O$, so $CD$ is a diameter and $CD=4$.
Diagonals $AB$ and $CD$ are perpendicular, so area $=\frac12 d_1d_2=\frac12\times4\times\sqrt{14}=2\sqrt{14}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Find $A,B,C,D$ explicitly and use the area of a quadrilateral as half the cross product of its diagonal vectors.
solution: The line $y=x$ meets the circle at $C=(\sqrt2,\sqrt2)$ and $D=(-\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)$; $\vec{CD}=(-2\sqrt2,-2\sqrt2)$.
For the quadrilateral $ADBC$ with diagonals $AB$ and $CD$: area $=\frac12\left|\vec{AB}\times\vec{CD}\right|$.

useful_results: The perpendicular through the mid-point of any chord passes through the centre (perpendicular bisector of a chord).
Area of any quadrilateral $=\frac12 d_1d_2\sin\theta$ between its diagonals; $=\frac12d_1d_2$ when they are perpendicular.
Chord of length $2\sqrt{r^2-p^2}$ at distance $p$ from the centre; here $p=\frac{|c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ for the line $ax+by+c=0$ through $x^2+y^2=r^2$.

concepts: Circle through two points with centre on a line
Length of a chord with given mid-point
questions.question: Let a circle $C$ pass through the points $(4,2)$ and $(0,2)$, and its centre lie on $3x+2y+2=0$. Then the length of the chord, of the circle $C$, whose mid-point is $(1,2)$, is:
questions.key_idea: The centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of the chord joining the two given points, here the vertical line $x=2$.
solution: The chord joining $A(4,2)$ and $B(0,2)$ has slope $0$, so the centre $O$ lies on its perpendicular bisector, which is vertical through the mid-point $(2,2)$: $x=2$.
The centre is $\left(\alpha,\frac{-2-3\alpha}{2}\right)$ on $3x+2y+2=0$; $OM$ vertical gives $\alpha=2$.
The mid-point of the required chord is $N(1,2)$, so $ON=\sqrt{(2-1)^2+(-4-2)^2}=\sqrt{37}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: For a chord with mid-point $N$ the half-chord squared equals $-S(N)$, the negative of the power of $N$.
solution: The centre is $(2,-4)$ as before, so the circle is $x^2+y^2-4x+8y+c=0$.
If $N$ is the mid-point of a chord, then (half chord)$^2$ $=NP\cdot NQ=-S(N)=3$.

useful_results: Centre of a circle through two points lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.
For a chord with mid-point $N$ inside the circle: (half chord)$^2=r^2-ON^2=-S(N)$, so length $=2\sqrt{-S_{11}}$.
Instance: $S(1,2)=-3$ gives half chord $\sqrt3$, matching $r^2-ON^2=40-37$.

concepts: Square inscribed in a circle
Parallel lines at a given distance from the centre
questions.question: A square is inscribed in the circle $x^2+y^2-10x-6y+30=0$. One side of this square is parallel to $y=x+3$. If $(x_i,y_i)$ are the vertices of the square, then $\sum\left(x_i^2+y_i^2\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: A side of the inscribed square is at distance $r/\sqrt2$ from the centre, which fixes the two parallel sides.
solution: The half-diagonal of the square is $r=2$, so the distance from the centre to a side is $\frac{2}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$.
Sides parallel to $y=x+3$ are $x-y+c=0$; distance from $(5,3)$: $\frac{|5-3+c|}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$.
The two lines are $y=x$ and $y=x-4$; solve each with the circle.

alternate_solutions.idea: Vertices are $c+r\,u_i$ with $\sum u_i=0$ for a square, so $\sum|v_i|^2=4(|c|^2+r^2)$ without finding any vertex.
solution: Let the centre be $c=(5,3)$ and $r=2$; the vertices of an inscribed square are $v_i=c+r\,u_i$ with unit vectors $u_i=\pm u,\pm u^{\perp}$.
The direction of the side (parallel to $y=x+3$) is not needed.

useful_results: For any square (or regular polygon) inscribed in a circle of centre $c$, radius $r$: $\sum|v_i|^2=n\left(|c|^2+r^2\right)$.
Distance from the centre to a side of an inscribed square is $r/\sqrt2$; side length $r\sqrt2$.
Circle $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+c=0$ has $r^2=g^2+f^2-c$.

concepts: Chord of a circle and distance from the centre
Distance between parallel lines
questions.question: Let $C$ be a circle with radius $\sqrt{10}$ units and centre at the origin. Let the line $x+y=2$ intersect the circle $C$ at the points $P$ and $Q$. Let $MN$ be a chord of $C$ of length $2$ unit and slope $-1$. Then, a distance (in units) between the chord $PQ$ and the chord $MN$ is:
questions.key_idea: A chord of length $2$ in a circle of radius $\sqrt{10}$ lies at distance $3$ from the centre, and $MN\parallel PQ$.
solution: Let $A$ be the mid-point of $MN$; $AN=\frac{MN}{2}=1$ and $OA\perp MN$.
Perpendicular distance of the centre from $PQ$: $\frac{|0+0-2|}{\sqrt2}=\sqrt2$.
$MN$ and $PQ$ both have slope $-1$, so they are parallel; the distance between them is $OA+\sqrt2$ or $|OA-\sqrt2|$ depending on the side of $O$ on which $MN$ lies.
So the distance is $3+\sqrt2$ or $3-\sqrt2$; only $3-\sqrt2$ is among the options: (C).

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $MN$ as $x+y=k$ and impose chord length $2$ algebraically; the distance between the parallel lines is $\frac{|k-2|}{\sqrt2}$.
solution: Since the line has slope $-1$, $MN^2=2(x_1-x_2)^2=2(20-k^2)=4$, so $k^2=18$, $k=\pm3\sqrt2$.
This gives $3-\sqrt2$ for $k=3\sqrt2$ and $3+\sqrt2$ for $k=-3\sqrt2$; the option is $3-\sqrt2$.

useful_results: A chord of length $\ell$ in a circle of radius $R$ lies at distance $\sqrt{R^2-\ell^2/4}$ from the centre.
Parallel chords lie at signed distances $d_1,d_2$ from the centre; the gap is $|d_1-d_2|$ (same side) or $d_1+d_2$ (opposite sides) - check both against the options.
Two lines $ax+by=c_1$, $ax+by=c_2$ are $\frac{|c_1-c_2|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}$ apart.

concepts: Circle touching two lines
Shortest distance of a point from a circle
questions.question: Let a circle $C$ of radius $1$ and closer to the origin be such that the lines passing through the point $(3,2)$ and parallel to the coordinate axes touch it. Then the shortest distance of the circle $C$ from the point $(5,5)$ is:
questions.key_idea: Tangent lines $x=3$ and $y=2$ put the centre at distance $1$ from both; the shortest distance to an outside point is $d-r$.
solution: The lines through $(3,2)$ parallel to the axes are $x=3$ and $y=2$; both touch the circle of radius $1$.
So the centre is at distance $1$ from each: $(3\pm1,\,2\pm1)$; the one closest to the origin is $(2,1)$.
The point is outside the circle, so the minimum distance $=5-1=4$.
useful_results: Shortest distance from an outside point $P$ to a circle (centre $C$, radius $r$) is $PC-r$; the longest is $PC+r$.
A circle of radius $r$ touching the lines $x=p$ and $y=q$ has centre $(p\pm r,\,q\pm r)$: four possible circles.
Instance: $(2,1)$ and $(5,5)$ form a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle.

concepts: Circle touching two perpendicular lines
Squares and diagonals (coordinate geometry)
questions.question: Let $ABCD$ and $AEFG$ be squares of side $4$ and $2$ units, respectively. Then point $E$ is on the line segment $AB$ and the point $F$ is on the diagonal $AC$. Then the radius $r$ of the circle passing through the point $F$ and touching the line segments $BC$ and $CD$ satisfies:
questions.key_idea: A circle touching $BC$ and $CD$ has its centre on the diagonal $AC$, so $CF=r\sqrt2+r$.
solution: A circle touching $BC$ and $CD$ has its centre on the diagonal $AC$ at distance $r\sqrt2$ from $C$.
$F$ lies on the circle and on the diagonal, on the side of the centre away from $C$: $CF=r\sqrt2+r$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Coordinates with $A$ at the origin: the centre is $(4-r,4-r)$ and $F=(2,2)$ must satisfy the circle equation.
solution: A circle inside the square touching $BC$ ($x=4$) and $CD$ ($y=4$) has centre $(4-r,4-r)$.
Roots $4\pm2\sqrt2$; the root $4+2\sqrt2>4$ would put the centre outside the square, so $r=4-2\sqrt2$.

useful_results: A circle touching two intersecting lines has its centre on an angle bisector; for perpendicular lines the centre is at distance $r\sqrt2$ from the vertex.
Diagonal of a square of side $s$ is $s\sqrt2$; a point on the diagonal is easiest to handle as $(t,t)$.
Tangent circle in the corner of a square: centre $(s-r,s-r)$, so any point $(p,p)$ on the circle gives $2(s-r-p)^2=r^2$.

concepts: Radical axis (common chord) of two circles
questions.question: Let the circle $C_1:\ x^2+y^2-2(x+y)+1=0$ and $C_2$ be a circle having centre at $(-1,0)$ and radius $2$. If the line of common chord of $C_1$ and $C_2$ intersects the $y$-axis at the point $P$, then the square of the distance of $P$ from the centre of $C_1$ is:
questions.key_idea: The common chord is the radical axis $S_1-S_2=0$.
solution: Distance of $P$ from the centre of $C_1$: $\sqrt{(1-0)^2+(1-2)^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $P$ on the radical axis has equal powers with respect to both circles; impose this for $P=(0,y)$.
solution: On the common chord the powers are equal: $(y-1)^2=y^2-3$, so $-2y+1=-3$ and $y=2$.

useful_results: Two intersecting circles $S_1=0$, $S_2=0$: common chord is $S_1-S_2=0$ (when the coefficients of $x^2,y^2$ are $1$).
Every point of the radical axis has equal power with respect to both circles.
Circles with centres $d$ apart and radii $r_1,r_2$ intersect in two points iff $|r_1-r_2|<d<r_1+r_2$; here $1<\sqrt5<3$.

concepts: Incircle of an equilateral triangle
Square inscribed in a circle
questions.question: A circle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle of side of length $12$. If the area and perimeter of any square inscribed in this circle are $m$ and $n$, respectively, then $m+n^2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Inradius $r=\Delta/s$; a square in a circle of radius $r$ has diagonal $2r$.
solution: Let the side of the square be $a$; its diagonal is the diameter, so $2a^2=4r^2$.
For an equilateral triangle of side $12$, the inradius is $r=\frac{12}{2\sqrt3}=2\sqrt3$, so $r^2=12$.
A square inscribed in a circle of radius $r$ has side $r\sqrt2$: area $m=2r^2$, perimeter $n=4\sqrt2\,r$.

useful_results: Equilateral triangle of side $a$: inradius $\frac{a}{2\sqrt3}$, circumradius $\frac{a}{\sqrt3}$, and $R=2r$.
Square inscribed in a circle of radius $r$: side $r\sqrt2$, area $2r^2$, perimeter $4\sqrt2\,r$.
Inradius of any triangle: $r=\Delta/s$.

concepts: Externally touching circles
Section formula (internal division)
questions.question: Let the circles $C_1:(x-\alpha)^2+(y-\beta)^2=r_1^2$ and $C_2:(x-8)^2+\left(y-\frac{15}{2}\right)^2=r_2^2$ touch each other externally at the point $(6,6)$. If the point $(6,6)$ divides the line segment joining the centres of the circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ internally in the ratio $2:1$, then $(\alpha+\beta)+4\left(r_1^2+r_2^2\right)$ equals:
questions.key_idea: The point of contact lies on the line of centres, so the section formula gives the unknown centre.
solution: $P(6,6)$ divides $C_1(\alpha,\beta)$ and $C_2\left(8,\frac{15}{2}\right)$ internally in the ratio $2:1$.
useful_results: Circles touching externally at $P$: $P$ lies on the line of centres and divides it internally as $C_1P:PC_2=r_1:r_2$ (for internal touching it divides externally in this ratio).
Here the ratio $2:1$ forces $r_1=2r_2$; check: $5=2\times\frac52$ and $C_1C_2=7.5=r_1+r_2$.
Section formula: $P=\frac{mC_2+nC_1}{m+n}$ when $C_1P:PC_2=m:n$.

concepts: Intercept form of a line and minimisation (application of derivatives)
Centre of a circle
questions.question: Let a variable line passing through the centre of the circle $x^2+y^2-16x-4y=0$, meet the positive co-ordinate axes at the points $A$ and $B$. Then the minimum value of $OA+OB$, where $O$ is the origin, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Minimise the sum of intercepts of a line through the fixed point $(8,2)$.
solution: A line through the centre: $y-2=m(x-8)$; to meet the positive axes the slope must be negative, $m<0$.
$f''(m)=-\frac{4}{m^3}>0$ for $m<0$, so this is a minimum.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's second line writes the circle as $(x-4)^2+(y-2)^2=20$; completing squares on $x^2-16x$ gives $(x-8)^2+(y-2)^2=68$. The PDF's next line already uses the correct centre $(8,2)$, so the answer 18 is unaffected. A check that $m<0$ and that the critical point is a minimum was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: Intercept form $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$ through $(8,2)$ and a Cauchy-Schwarz / AM-GM bound on $a+b$.
solution: Let the intercepts be $a=OA>0$, $b=OB>0$; the line $\frac xa+\frac yb=1$ passes through $(8,2)$, so $\frac8a+\frac2b=1$.
Equality when $\frac{8b}{a}=\frac{2a}{b}$, i.e. $a=2b$; then $\frac{4}{b}+\frac2b=1$ gives $b=6$, $a=12$ - both positive.
Minimum $OA+OB=18$ (slope $=-\frac{6}{12}=-\frac12$, as in the calculus method).

useful_results: For a line through $(p,q)$ with positive intercepts, $\min(a+b)=\left(\sqrt p+\sqrt q\right)^2$, attained when $a=p+\sqrt{pq}$, $b=q+\sqrt{pq}$.
Likewise the minimum of the area $\frac12ab$ is $2pq$ (at $a=2p$, $b=2q$); minimum of the segment length uses $\left(p^{2/3}+q^{2/3}\right)^{3/2}$.

concepts: Locus of mid-points of chords of a circle
Length of a chord
questions.question: Let the locus of the midpoints of the chords of the circle $x^2+(y-1)^2=1$ drawn from the origin intersect the line $x+y=1$ at $P$ and $Q$. Then, the length of $PQ$ is:
questions.key_idea: A chord through the origin satisfies $T=S_1$ for its mid-point; the origin on it gives the locus directly.
solution: Let the mid-point of the chord be $(h,k)$. The circle is $x^2+y^2-2y=0$.
The chord passes through the origin: $-k=h^2+k^2-2k$, so $h^2+k^2-k=0$.
Locus: $x^2+y^2-y=0$, a circle with centre $\left(0,\frac12\right)$ and radius $\frac12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: The mid-point $M$ of a chord through $O$ satisfies $CM\perp OM$ ($C$ the centre), so $M$ lies on the circle with diameter $OC$ (Thales).
solution: The centre of the given circle is $C(0,1)$.
For a chord through $O$ with mid-point $M$, the line from the centre to the mid-point is perpendicular to the chord: $\angle OMC=90^\circ$.
So $M$ lies on the circle with diameter $OC$: centre $\left(0,\frac12\right)$, radius $\frac12$ (equation $x^2+y^2-y=0$).

useful_results: Mid-points of chords of a circle through a fixed point $Q$ lie on the circle with diameter $QC$ ($C$ = centre).
Chord with mid-point $(h,k)$: $T=S_1$.
Locus of mid-points of chords of fixed length $\ell$: a concentric circle of radius $\sqrt{R^2-\ell^2/4}$.

concepts: Locus of a point dividing a moving chord in a ratio
Parametric form of a point on a circle
questions.question: A line segment $AB$ of length $\lambda$ moves such that the points $A$ and $B$ remain on the periphery of a circle of radius $\lambda$. Then the locus of the point that divides the line segment $AB$ in the ratio $2:3$ is a circle of radius:
questions.key_idea: A chord equal to the radius subtends $60^\circ$ at the centre, so $\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)=\frac12$.
solution: Take the centre at the origin: $A=(\lambda\cos\theta_2,\lambda\sin\theta_2)$, $B=(\lambda\cos\theta_1,\lambda\sin\theta_1)$ and $AB=\lambda$.
The locus $h^2+k^2=\frac{19\lambda^2}{25}$ is a circle of radius $\frac{\lambda}{5}\sqrt{19}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Triangle $OAB$ is equilateral; drop $OM\perp AB$ and use Pythagoras for $OP$.
solution: Let $M$ be the mid-point of $AB$: $OM\perp AB$ and $OM=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\lambda$.
$OP=\frac{\sqrt{19}}{5}\lambda$ is constant, so $P$ moves on a circle of that radius.

useful_results: A chord of length equal to the radius subtends $60^\circ$ at the centre (equilateral triangle).
Chord of length $\ell$ in a circle of radius $R$, point $P$ dividing it as $m:n$: $OP^2=R^2-\frac{mn}{(m+n)^2}\ell^2$ (the locus is a concentric circle).
Instance: $\lambda^2-\frac{6}{25}\lambda^2=\frac{19}{25}\lambda^2$.

concepts: Locus of a point dividing a chord in a ratio
Parametric form of a point on a circle
questions.question: Let $A$ be the point $(1,2)$ and $B$ be any point on the curve $x^2+y^2=16$. If the centre of the locus of the point $P$, which divides the line segment $AB$ in the ratio $3:2$ is the point $C(\alpha,\beta)$, then the length of the line segment $AC$ is:
questions.key_idea: $P=A+\frac35(B-A)$ is a scaled copy of the circle, so its centre is easy to read off.
solution: Let $B=(4\cos\theta,4\sin\theta)$. $P(h,k)$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $3:2$, so $P=\frac{3B+2A}{5}$.
Squaring and adding: the locus of $P$ is $(5x-2)^2+(5y-4)^2=144$.

alternate_solutions.idea: $P=A+\frac35(B-A)$ is the image of $B$ under a homothety with centre $A$ and ratio $\frac35$, so the centre $O$ of the circle goes to $C$.
solution: The map $B\mapsto P=A+\frac35(B-A)$ is a homothety with centre $A$ and ratio $\frac35$.
It sends the circle $x^2+y^2=16$ (centre $O$, radius $4$) to a circle of radius $\frac{12}{5}$ whose centre is the image of $O$.

useful_results: If $B$ moves on a circle (centre $O$, radius $R$) and $P$ divides $AB$ in the ratio $m:n$ (from $A$), the locus of $P$ is a circle with centre $\frac{nA+mO}{m+n}$ and radius $\frac{m}{m+n}R$.
Instance: $\frac{2A+3O}{5}=\left(\frac25,\frac45\right)$ and radius $\frac35\cdot4=\frac{12}{5}$ (matches $(5x-2)^2+(5y-4)^2=144$).
Homothety maps circles to circles and centres to centres.

concepts: Tangents and normal of a circle
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the centre of a circle be $(\alpha,\beta)$ and its radius $r<8$. Let $3x+4y=24$ and $3x-4y=32$ be two tangents and $4x+3y=1$ be a normal to $C$. Then $(\alpha-\beta+r)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The centre is equidistant from the two tangents and lies on the normal; reject the second solution using $r<8$.
solution: The normal $4x+3y=1$ meets $3x-4y=32$ at $A(4,-5)$ (the normals are perpendicular, so $A$ is the point of contact of that tangent).
The centre $(\alpha,\beta)$ lies on the normal: $4\alpha+3\beta=1$, so $\beta=\frac{1-4\alpha}{3}$.
Distances to the two tangents are equal: $\frac{|3\alpha-4\beta-32|}{5}=\frac{|3\alpha+4\beta-24|}{5}$.
questions.correction_note: For $\alpha=\frac{28}{3}$ the PDF gives the centre $\left(\frac{28}{3},-\frac{109}{2}\right)$ and radius $\approx49.78$. With $\beta=\frac{1-4\alpha}{3}$ the correct values are $\beta=-\frac{109}{9}$ and $r=\frac{80}{9}\approx8.89$. This root is still rejected by $r<8$, so the answer 7 is unchanged. The intermediate equation $|25\alpha-100|=|7\alpha+68|$ was added.

alternate_solutions.idea: The two tangents have slopes $\pm\frac34$, so their angle bisectors are the lines $y=-1$ and $x=\frac{28}{3}$ through their meeting point; the centre is on one of them.
solution: Adding and subtracting the tangents: they meet at $T\left(\frac{28}{3},-1\right)$.
Their slopes are $-\frac34$ and $+\frac34$, symmetric about the horizontal line through $T$; so the angle bisectors are $y=-1$ and $x=\frac{28}{3}$.
The centre lies on a bisector and on the normal $4x+3y=1$: $y=-1$ gives $(1,-1)$; $x=\frac{28}{3}$ gives $\left(\frac{28}{3},-\frac{109}{9}\right)$.
Half-angle between the tangents and the horizontal bisector: $\tan\varphi=\frac34$, $\sin\varphi=\frac35$. For $(1,-1)$: $TC=\frac{25}{3}$, $r=TC\sin\varphi=5$.
For the other centre: $TC=\frac{100}{9}$ and the angle with the vertical bisector has sine $\frac45$, giving $r=\frac{80}{9}>8$, rejected.

useful_results: The centre of a circle touching two lines lies on one of the two angle bisectors of the lines; the bisectors are $\frac{L_1}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2}}=\pm\frac{L_2}{\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2}}$.
A normal to a circle passes through its centre; if it is perpendicular to a tangent it meets it at the point of contact.
Two tangents meeting at $T$ at angle $2\varphi$: $r=TC\sin\varphi$ for the centre $C$ on the bisector.

concepts: Locus of mid-points of chords subtending a given angle at the centre
Trigonometric equations
questions.question: The locus of the mid points of the chords of the circle $C_1:(x-4)^2+(y-5)^2=4$ which subtend an angle $\theta_i$ at the centre of the circle $C_1$, is a circle of radius $r_i$. If $\theta_1=\frac\pi3$, $\theta_3=\frac{2\pi}{3}$ and $r_1^2=r_2^2+r_3^2$, then $\theta_2$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The mid-point of a chord subtending $\theta$ at the centre is at distance $R\cos\frac\theta2$ from it.
solution: If a chord of a circle of radius $R$ subtends $\theta_i$ at the centre, the locus of its mid-point is a circle of radius $r_i=R\cos\frac{\theta_i}{2}$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF's third line writes the second and third terms both as $\cos^2\frac{\theta_2}{2}$ (they should be $\cos^2\frac{\theta_2}{2}$ and $\cos^2\frac{\theta_3}{2}$), and its last line concludes '$\therefore\theta_3=\frac\pi2$'; the quantity asked is $\theta_2=\frac\pi2$ ($\theta_3$ is given as $\frac{2\pi}{3}$). The answer (D) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use $\cos^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}$ so the condition becomes linear in $\cos\theta_i$.
solution: For the angle subtended by a chord, $0<\theta_2<\pi$, so $\theta_2=\frac\pi2$.

useful_results: The mid-point of a chord subtending angle $\theta$ at the centre of a circle of radius $R$ is at distance $R\cos\frac\theta2$ from the centre; the locus is a concentric circle.
$\cos^2\frac\theta2=\frac{1+\cos\theta}{2}$ turns sums of squares of half-angle cosines into sums of $\cos\theta$.
The locus of mid-points of chords of fixed length is likewise a concentric circle (here $\theta$ fixed).

concepts: Circle with a given diameter
Image (reflection) of a circle in a line
questions.question: The points of intersection of the line $ax+by=0$, $(a\ne b)$ and the circle $x^2+y^2-2x=0$ are $A(\alpha,0)$ and $B(1,\beta)$. The image of the circle with $AB$ as a diameter in the line $x+y+2=0$ is:
questions.key_idea: The conditions $a\ne b$, $B$ on the circle force $\alpha=0$ and $\beta=1$, so $A(0,0)$, $B(1,1)$.
solution: $A(\alpha,0)$ lies on $ax+by=0$, so $a\alpha=0$; $a\ne0$ (otherwise the line would be $y=0$ and $B$ would not be on the circle), hence $\alpha=0$.
$B(1,\beta)$ is on the line: $\beta=-\frac ab$; on the circle: $1+\beta^2-2=0$, so $\beta^2=1$.
Then $a^2=b^2$ and $a\ne b$, so $a+b=0$ and $\beta=-\frac ab=1$.
The circle with diameter $AB$, $A(0,0)$, $B(1,1)$, has centre $\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$ and radius $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$.
Image of the centre in $x+y+2=0$: $\frac{x-\frac12}{1}=\frac{y-\frac12}{1}=-2\cdot\frac{\frac12+\frac12+2}{2}=-3$, so the image is $\left(-\frac52,-\frac52\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflect the end-points of the diameter and write the circle in diameter form $(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$.
solution: With $A(0,0)$, $B(1,1)$ as before, reflect them in $x+y+2=0$.
$A'B'$ is a diameter of the image circle: $(x+2)(x+3)+(y+2)(y+3)=0$.

useful_results: Image of a circle in a line is a circle of the same radius whose centre is the image of the centre; reflect only the centre (or two ends of a diameter).
Image of $(x_1,y_1)$ in $ax+by+c=0$: $\frac{x-x_1}{a}=\frac{y-y_1}{b}=-\frac{2(ax_1+by_1+c)}{a^2+b^2}$.
Circle with $(x_1,y_1)$, $(x_2,y_2)$ as ends of a diameter: $(x-x_1)(x-x_2)+(y-y_1)(y-y_2)=0$.

concepts: Pair of tangents and chord of contact (pole and polar)
Distance of a point from a line
questions.question: Let the tangents at the points $A(4,-11)$ and $B(8,-5)$ on the circle $x^2+y^2-3x+10y-15=0$, intersect at the point $C$. Then the radius of the circle, whose centre is $C$ and the line joining $A$ and $B$ is its tangent, is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $AB$ is the polar (chord of contact) of $C$, so comparing it with the polar of $C(h,k)$ gives $C$.
solution: Let $C=(h,k)$. The chord of contact of $C$ ($T=0$): $hx+ky-\frac32(x+h)+5(y+k)-15=0$.
The circle with centre $C$ touching $AB$ has radius equal to the distance from $C$ to $AB$: $\frac{|3\cdot8+\frac{56}{3}-34|}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{26/3}{\sqrt{13}}=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{3}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: In the right triangle $OAC$ (right angle at $A$) the foot of the altitude $AM$ is the mid-point of $AB$, and $AM^2=OM\cdot MC$.
solution: $CA\perp OA$, and $AM\perp OC$ ($M$ on $OC$), so in the right triangle $OAC$: $AM^2=OM\cdot MC$.
$MC=\frac{13}{\frac{3\sqrt{13}}{2}}=\frac{26}{3\sqrt{13}}=\frac{2\sqrt{13}}{3}$, which is the distance from $C$ to $AB$, i.e. the required radius.

useful_results: The chord of contact (polar) of an external point $(x_1,y_1)$ w.r.t. $S=0$ is $T=0$; to find the pole of a given chord, compare $T=0$ with the chord.
If tangents from $C$ touch at $A,B$ and $M$ is the mid-point of $AB$: $OM\cdot OC=R^2$ and $AM^2=OM\cdot MC$.
Distance of the pole $C$ from its chord of contact: $CM=\frac{CA^2}{CO}$ (tangent length squared over the distance to the centre).

concepts: Circle touching three lines (incircle of a triangle)
Angle bisector and altitude of an isosceles triangle
questions.question: Let $y=x+2$, $4y=3x+6$ and $3y=4x+1$ be three tangent lines to the circle $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$. Then $h+k$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The three lines form an isosceles triangle ($AB=AC$), so the bisector from $A$ is the altitude and is the line $x+y=5$.
solution: Vertices: $4y=3x+6$ and $3y=4x+1$ meet at $A(2,3)$; $y=x+2$ meets $4y=3x+6$ at $B(-2,0)$ and $3y=4x+1$ at $C(5,7)$.
$\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $AB=AC$, so the bisector of $\angle A$ and the altitude from $A$ coincide.
$BC$ ($x-y+2=0$) has slope $1$, so the altitude from $A$ has slope $-1$: $x+y=\lambda$ through $A(2,3)$, so $\lambda=5$.
The centre of the (in)circle lies on the bisector of $\angle A$, i.e. on $x+y=5$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF does not say which circle is meant. Three lines have four tangent circles (incircle and three excircles): the incentre and the excentre opposite $A$ both lie on $x+y=5$ ($h+k=5$), the excentre opposite $B$ gives $h+k=5+5\sqrt2$ and the one opposite $C$ gives $5-5\sqrt2$. The PDF's working is only valid for the incircle, so a step stating that the centre is on the bisector of $\angle A$ was added. The key (A) $5$ is kept, but the question is ambiguous.

alternate_solutions.idea: Bisect the pair of lines $3x-4y+6=0$ and $4x-3y+1=0$ directly: the bisectors are $x+y=5$ and $x-y+1=0$, without finding any vertex.
solution: Equal-distance condition for the lines $3x-4y+6=0$ and $4x-3y+1=0$ (both have $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=5$): $3x-4y+6=\pm(4x-3y+1)$.
The $+$ sign gives $x+y=5$; the $-$ sign gives $x-y+1=0$.
The second bisector is parallel to the third tangent $x-y+2=0$ (distance $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$ from it), which would force excircles with centres $h-k=-1$.
The in-circle (and the $A$-excircle) lie on $x+y=5$, so $h+k=5$.
Check with the incentre formula: $I=\frac{7\sqrt2(2,3)+5(-2,0)+5(5,7)}{7\sqrt2+10}$ gives $h+k=\frac{35\sqrt2+50}{7\sqrt2+10}=5$.

useful_results: Three lines in general position have four tangent circles: the incircle and three excircles of the triangle they form.
In an isosceles triangle ($AB=AC$) the bisector of $\angle A$, the median and the altitude from $A$ coincide.
Bisectors of $a_1x+b_1y+c_1=0$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2=0$: $\frac{a_1x+b_1y+c_1}{\sqrt{a_1^2+b_1^2}}=\pm\frac{a_2x+b_2y+c_2}{\sqrt{a_2^2+b_2^2}}$.

concepts: Tangent to a circle and rolling along it
Reflection (image) of a point in a line
Area of a trapezium
questions.question: Let a circle $C_1$ be obtained on rolling the circle $x^2+y^2-4x-6y+11=0$ upwards $4$ units on the tangent $T$ to it at the point $(3,2)$. Let $C_2$ be the image of $C_1$ in $T$. Let $A$ and $B$ be the centres of circles $C_1$ and $C_2$ respectively, and $M$ and $N$ be respectively the feet of perpendiculars drawn from $A$ and $B$ on the $x$-axis. Then the area of the trapezium $AMNB$ is:
questions.key_idea: Rolling along $T$ keeps the centre at distance $r$ from $T$, so $A$ moves $4$ units along $T$ and $B=A+2r\hat n$.
solution: The radius to $(3,2)$ has direction $(1,-1)$, so the tangent $T$ has direction $(1,1)$: $T:\ x-y-1=0$.
Rolling upwards $4$ units along $T$ moves the centre by $4\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,1)$: $A=\left(2+2\sqrt2,\,3+2\sqrt2\right)$.
$C_2$ is the image of $C_1$ in $T$. $A$ is at distance $r=\sqrt2$ from $T$, so $B=A+2\sqrt2\cdot\frac{(1,-1)}{\sqrt2}=A+(2,-2)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Only $y_A$ matters: $AM\parallel BN$ and $MN=x_B-x_A=2$, so the area is $\frac12(y_A+y_B)\cdot2=y_A+y_B$.
solution: $A$ and $B$ are mirror images in $T$ ($x-y-1=0$), at distance $\sqrt2$ on opposite sides, so $\vec{AB}=2\sqrt2\cdot\frac{(1,-1)}{\sqrt2}=(2,-2)$.
The parallel sides are $AM=y_A$ and $BN=y_B=y_A-2$; the height is $MN=x_B-x_A=2$.

useful_results: Rolling a circle along a tangent line moves its centre parallel to the line, keeping it at distance $r$ from it.
Image of a point at distance $d$ from a line is at distance $d$ on the other side, along the normal: $B=A\pm2d\,\hat n$.
Area of the trapezium with parallel sides $p,q$ and distance $h$ between them is $\frac12(p+q)h$; with sides perpendicular to an axis, the height is the difference of $x$-coordinates.
